podcast.title: Royalty Lawsuit Defense (1998)
podcast.body: In a 1998 lawsuit brought by The Ronettes for unpaid royalties, Phil Spector argued that he owed them nothing and, in fact, they still owed him money. His defense was based on the claim that the costs of recording their singles had always exceeded the revenue they generated. "In court Specter argued that he didn't owe them any more, and indeed that they still owed him money, because the cost of recording their singles meant that they had never actually earned more money than they cost."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Murder Conviction (2003)
podcast.body: The host notes that Phil Spector murdered a woman in 2003, implying that his subsequent conviction was not surprising given his history of abusive and controlling behavior, particularly towards Ronnie Spector. "I was completely unsurprised when he murdered a woman in 2003."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: "Wall of Sound" Production Style and Rejection of "Don't Worry Baby" (1960s)
podcast.body: Brian Wilson deeply admired Phil Spector's iconic "Wall of Sound" production style, especially evident in The Ronettes' "Be My Baby," and often sought to emulate or adapt it for The Beach Boys, eventually developing a variant emphasizing "gentle fragility." Spector notably declined to record "Don't Worry Baby" for The Ronettes, leading The Beach Boys to record it themselves. "F Edwards, Alex please Phil Spectre turned the song down and so the beach boys recorded it themselves."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 117: "Don't Worry Baby" by the Beach Boys

podcast.title: Accused of Stealing Ideas by Joe Meek
podcast.body: During a period of his deteriorating mental health and increasing paranoia, Joe Meek once received a call from Phil Spector. Meek furiously hung up on Spector, vehemently accusing him of stealing his musical ideas and production techniques. "En una ocasión recibió una llamada de Phil Spector, Mick le colgó un farado acusándole de robarle sus ideas."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: El productor que escuchó el nuevo mundo. Joe Meek.

podcast.title: B-side Strategy for Singles
podcast.body: Phil Spector, known for his controlling tendencies, frequently used instrumental jam sessions by studio musicians as B-sides for his singles. He would credit himself as the songwriter for these tracks, a tactic intended to deter DJs from playing the B-side instead of the A-side hit. "Spectre was enough of a control freak that he didn't want DJs ever to play the wrong side of his singles, so he stuck instrumental jam sessions by the studio musicians, with the songwriting credited to him rather than to them. On the B sides."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.body: During the unraveling of the Smile project, Brian Wilson's paranoia grew to the extent that he believed he was the target of a conspiracy led by Phil Spector. "incluso llegó a pensar que era el blanco de una conspiración encabezada por Fille Spector."

podcast.body: Phil Spector is currently serving time in prison for the shooting death of actress Lana Clarkson. "Phil Specter, serving time for the shooting death of Lana Clarkson."

podcast.title: Fairfax High School Rivalry
podcast.body: Phil Specter attended Fairfax High, a school with a strong rivalry with University High. Like University High, Fairfax High also produced numerous famous individuals, contributing to the vibrant music and entertainment scene in Los Angeles. "Specter went to Fairfax High, a school which had a strong rivalry with University High, and produced a similarly ludicrous list of famous people."

podcast.title: First Appearance on Coasters Record
podcast.body: Phil Spector's first appearance on a Coasters record was on "Shopping for Clothes," marking the beginning of his collaboration with Lieber and Stoller. "It's also notable for being the first coasters record to feature a young musician that Leibor and Stuller were mentoring of the time."

podcast.title: Infamous Career Trajectory
podcast.body: Specter's name became infamous due to his legal troubles. He died in prison in 2021, where he had been incarcerated for a dozen years after being convicted for the murder of actress Lana Clarkson. "Of course, the name Phil Specter is now also infamous."

podcast.title: Legendary "Wall of Sound" Producer
podcast.body: Phil Specter was known as a "legendary wall of sound producer" who worked with a wide range of artists, including The Ronettes, Tina Turner, and The Righteous Brothers. "The legendary wall of sound producer worked with everyone from the Ronets to Tina Turner to the righteous brothers."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Mentored by Lieber & Stoller
podcast.body: Phil Spector, a young musician and a huge admirer of Jerry Lieber and Mike Stoller, was mentored by the duo. He sought to learn from them and was given an apprenticeship, receiving a publishing contract, jobs as a session guitarist, and temporary housing in their office or Lieber's spare room. "Lester Siller said that the kid in question was a huge admirer of Leibor and Stuller, and wanted to learn from them."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Musical Clique
podcast.body: Specter formed his own musical clique with friends like Marshall Leib (his best friend) and Marshall's girlfriend's younger brother, Loss Tittleman, with whom he made music. "he'd got his own little clique of people around him with whom he was making music."

podcast.title: Preventing Rock and Roll Hall of Fame Induction
podcast.body: While serving on the board of the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Phil Spector used his position to prevent The Ronettes' induction. This act of spite against his ex-wife, Ronnie Spector, continued until his imprisonment, after which the group was finally inducted in 2007. "Specter, who was on the board of the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, prevented the Vanette from being inducted out of spite towards his ex until he was imprisoned, at which point they were finally recognised in 2007."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.body: Brian Wilson aimed to emulate and surpass Phil Spector in production, reflecting Spector's highly influential status as a producer in the music industry during that era. "hace el espector en producción."

podcast.title: Ranked Below Joe Meek by NME
podcast.body: In 2014, the English magazine NME (New Musical Express) published a ranking naming Joe Meek the most important producer of all time. This influential ranking controversially placed him above renowned figures like Phil Spector. "Por encima de Phil Spector, Gwen Cillons, George Martin o Rick Rubin."

podcast.title: Rising Hitmaker Reputation
podcast.body: By the early 1960s, Phil Spector had established a strong reputation in the music industry as a hitmaker, successfully producing records for groups like The Crystals, The Blossoms, and studio groups such as Bobby Soxx and the Blue Jeans, as well as working freelance for artists like Connie Francis. "Specter was becoming very well known in the music industry as a hitmaker."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Solo Instrumental Project (as Phil Harvey)
podcast.body: Specter, growing disenchanted with The Teddy Bears, created a solo instrumental single under the name "Phil Harvey." He then assembled the Phil Harvey band from former members of The Moon Dogs to perform a single promotional gig for this release. "The actor had become disenchanted with being in the teddy bears, and had put together a solo instrumental single under the name Phil Harvey."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Songwriting Contribution Debate
podcast.body: There is significant debate surrounding the extent of Phil Spector's songwriting contributions when he is co-credited. While some co-writers claim he would often only alter a word or phrase in an already completed song, others, like Barry Mann (who credited Spector with the middle section of "You've Lost That Lovin' Feeling"), suggest more substantial input, though he was rarely the primary writer. "Some of his co-writers have said that he would often only change a word or phrase and get himself cut in on an already completed song."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 110: "Be My Baby" by the Ronettes

podcast.title: Wall of Sound Production Method
podcast.body: Phil Spector was known for his immersive production through his "Wall of Sound" methods, developed in the early 1960s. These techniques typically resulted in upbeat, high-energy, and danceable songs. When working with George Harrison, however, he adapted this method to a more subdued style.

xref.body: The Ramones were great admirers of the 60s era "Nuggets bands."
